title: Animated history of a mechanism
byline: Jean Jabely · commentary by Raymond Queneau · 1956
line: Show what each invention makes possible through motion and consequence.
image: A cave-painting tableau with handprints and animal silhouettes
sources: The distributor identifies the 1956 Jabely animation and supplies the still.
Describes Queneau’s commentary and the dossier placing image descriptions beside it.
Prove a mechanism through a moving material assembly.
thesis: Make a machine’s problem intelligible through performance. Each change in mechanism must visibly alter what a body, wheel, or material can do. Let narration complicate that action with a joke or observation.
state: ◻(Mechanism) has sourced period, input force, moving parts, contact points, supported action, and failure mode. ◻(ExplanatoryBeat) pairs one visible movement with commentary and a sound event. [substitute] swaps the active mechanism while preserving the task it attempts.
invariant: Keep historical attribution tied to a source and mark staged compression. Preserve the same challenge across comparisons. Carry contact, force, and material limits through motion. Time a commentary joke to a visible causal beat.
concurrency: An illustrator and mechanic modeler can work from the same joint and contact definitions. Changing the transmission or wheel scale reopens animation checks for the corresponding beat. At 100×, eliminate variants without distinct mechanical outcomes before rendering.
swarm: A historian checks the small mechanism sequence. A layout artist designs repeated before/after framing. An animator makes contact and force readable. A commentary and sound unit aligns punchline and mechanical cue. An independent viewer reconstructs the causal improvement.
proof: Make 30 seconds of a load moved by dragging, rolling on loose cylinders, and riding on a simple wheeled platform. Present it as a demonstration of mechanisms and cite chronology only where sourced. Give one nonhuman object a brief commentary line. Make the improvement readable with sound off.
fixture: In a cycle, the same input force and geometry produce the declared motion or documented exception. Removing axle coupling must alter wheel-to-body movement. An unexplained jump in load position fails continuity.
critic: Ask which problem each mechanism solved and where commentary added a distinct idea. Compare the same staging with and without the commentary.
inquiry: If the middle mechanism is unreadable, lock sound and stage one contact in close-up. If it reads but the gag fails, retain motion and vary voice placement relative to effort.
branch: Replace the narrator with the load or the road. Preserve the mechanism and compare how the new perspective changes attention.
deliver: Playable animated mechanism study, parts and contact schema, historical source register, dual-column picture/commentary score, and a causal reading review.
shared: Let the station cart demonstrate the problem of transporting the sealed envelope or bench load. Stage the physical effect of a wheel or bearing while preserving the station events.

title: An impossible narrator and a working storyboard
byline: Jean Jabely and Raymond Queneau · c. 1958 dossier
line: Build a story from the friction between a witness and the machinery it observes.
image: A storyboard page with three drawings of early flying machines and handwritten annotations
sources: Describes the hand-drawn storyboard and Queneau’s aviation commentary spoken by a bird.
Make words, sounds, and physical action share precise cue intervals.
thesis: Use a narrator who possesses the ability humans are attempting to invent. Make the voice and image disclose different information about the same mechanical attempt.
state: ◻(Witness) has affordances, perceptual limits, and attitude. ◻(Attempt) records mechanism, action, material outcome, source or fiction status. ◻(StoryboardCue) joins image/transition and commentary/FX at a shared time anchor with a declared contrast.
invariant: Keep factual mechanism claims tied to evidence or make the scene visibly fictional. Maintain a stable narrator viewpoint. A crucial image and cue each contribute a distinct inference, and the animatic shows the attempt and consequence.
concurrency: Board and voice teams branch from the same attempt IDs. They can merge when the physical outcome and witness access remain consistent. Changing a success into a failure invalidates associated cue contrasts. At 100×, group pitches by witness-to-mechanism relationship.
swarm: An invention researcher records what a mechanism can do. A board artist designs readable poses and attempts. A writer builds the nonhuman account. A timing and sound unit tests voice against action. A fresh critic compares image-only, voice-only, and combined reads.
proof: Create a 25–35 second animatic about a bird watching a fictional inventor try a paper wing, a rubber-band rotor, and a failed glide. Show one particular failure as a short board sequence. Use the bird’s calm narration to reframe the event as a reasonable action from its own perspective.
fixture: Each board row resolves a frame range, source or fiction ID, observed action, and cue. Swapping narration between two rows is a valid experiment when the witness can observe both. Assigning knowledge from beyond its field or time fails the witness gate.
critic: Ask what the mechanism did in silence, what the narrator seems to value in audio, and what the combination adds. Locate the first frame where the physical failure can be understood.
inquiry: If the voice merely explains the drawing, keep the attempt and replace one comment with a different point of comparison. If the joke obscures the mechanism, compare a cue just before impact with one delayed until after recovery.
branch: Offer a second witness with a different natural ability. Compare what it notices about exactly the same attempt.
deliver: Playable animatic, frame-accurate dual-column board, voice and effects stems, evidence/fiction ledger, and independent review.
shared: Give the station bell or an observing bird a voice. Let it describe the visitor’s pause from the standpoint of its own abilities. Ground the visible acts in the unchanged event record.

title: One encounter across three eras
line: Make the same encounter legible as world, medium, and genre change.
image: A chicken on a sidewalk in the black-and-white portion of the film
gallery: The encounter in the brightly colored 2009 section
The chicken near a wrecked car in the 2059 section
sources: Documents the short and provides stills.
Grant Orchard interview, Animation World Network
Orchard names Queneau’s repetition as an inspiration and credits the chicken anecdote to a story in Paul Auster’s collection.
Keep staging readable across very different render representations.
thesis: Let a repeated small action accrue meaning through three different worlds. Preserve one unmistakable gesture while period, rendering method, environment, and genre change how the audience reads its consequence.
state: ◻(CoreBeat) has stable actor role, action, object, and causal predecessor. ◻(EraWorld) carries materials, available devices, hazards, and sound rules. ◻(Version) maps canonical beats into each world’s staging, timeline, and rendering pipeline.
invariant: Declare protected beats and their observable signatures before producing the eras. Each era renders them legibly. Let world-specific consequences differ only where the direction allows. Track time period, genre, and render technique as separate variables.
concurrency: Assign one candidate per era and a shared integration owner. Changing a protected beat or matched cue creates a new common revision. At 100×, compare one shared beat across style samples before building three complete pipelines.
swarm: A story editor freezes the encounter. Three small production branches express it through distinct staging and materials. A sound unit carries and transforms a recurring cue. An assembly editor checks accumulation. An independent viewer identifies the repeated event and changed stakes.
proof: Create three 12–18 second versions of someone watching an animal enter an unlikely place. Choose three eras and distinct visual systems. Match one action and one sound cue precisely enough to be recognized. Let the third version exploit a new environmental affordance.
fixture: The three manifests share required event IDs and the recurring gesture. A new plot can be a separate experiment. To isolate style, add a fourth diagnostic render of one era with alternate technique and unchanged event timing.
critic: Screen the triptych in order and ask what repeats, which new condition changes the stakes, and whether the third version earns its escalation. Then compare the diagnostic render to distinguish era from technique.
inquiry: If versions feel like filters, hold the gesture and redesign how the environment can answer it. If the audience loses the common action, use a stronger staging anchor before unifying color or sound.
branch: Try one new era with the same camera path as an existing version. Record what its materials and sound permit that the other world could not.
deliver: Three playable shorts and one assembly, cross-version beat map, era and material manifests, recurring cue stems, and a comparison anchored in playback.
shared: Put the station encounter in three eras. Keep the visitor, envelope, bell, discovery, and departure. Change the station materials and how the bell sounds. Preserve the key’s placement and the unopened door.

title: A grammar of retellings
line: Keep the incident fixed and give each retelling a different rule.
image: Yellow cover of the illustrated Gallimard Jeunesse edition of Exercices de style
sources: Identifies Queneau’s text and the later edition with contributions from many illustrators.
Describes Queneau’s many retellings of one everyday incident.
Treat transformations as named operators with declared effects.
thesis: Show that form changes what someone notices in an ordinary event. Every variant should use a rule the reader can infer from what it does to the telling.
state: ◻(Incident) has event IDs, causal dependencies, roles, and outcomes. ◻(StyleOperator) has input domain, protected facts, mutable dimensions, and executable or observable acceptance conditions. ◻(Retelling) links claims and omissions to source events.
invariant: Retain declared incident facts or make permitted omissions traceable. Preserve a baseline for comparison. Each variant has one primary operation and a declared relationship to the source. Variants with equivalent effects count as one approach when selecting work.
concurrency: Writers work from a frozen event ledger. Their drafts merge into an anthology by variant ID. A change in source facts creates a new baseline and reopens affected entries. At 100×, prune by operator signatures and fact coverage before commissioning readings.
swarm: An incident editor freezes the facts. Assign independent writers different operators. A constraint verifier runs coverage and applicable formal checks. An independent reader identifies what each form reveals or withholds.
proof: Write one original six-beat mundane incident and four short retellings: a log in reverse order, a witness’s sensory inventory, a notice with rigid format, and a version narrated by an object. Give every variant a demonstrably different transformation. Start with four and scale toward 99 only when new operators earn their place.
fixture: A reverse-order variant changes presentation order and preserves underlying causal edges. A sensory inventory may omit a cause if the observer lacks access and the omission is recorded. A version that invents a new ending fails the shared-incident comparison.
critic: Present the unlabeled variants and have a reader name what stayed stable, what new detail gained force, and which pair feels redundant. Run form-specific checks independently of judgment.
inquiry: If styles differ only in vocabulary, retain the incident and vary order, information access, or sentence constraint. If a variant becomes unintelligible, isolate one indispensable beat and test a cue that fits its rule.
branch: Carry one verbal operator into sound, comic layout, or edit timing. Specify which formal relation survives the move and demonstrate it with a small sample.
deliver: An original baseline, four readable variations, operator cards, coverage and constraint records, reader comparison, and a reproducible anthology source.
shared: Use the station record as the incident. Compare reverse chronology, a sensory inventory, an incident report, and the key as narrator. Preserve the facts of the departure.

title: One picture edit, two soundtracks
line: Play the same frames twice and let voice and music change their meaning.
image: Apartment blocks across a road in the documentary
sources: Describes the identical visual edit presented twice with different commentary and music.
Use speech, sound timing, and perceptual review as production state.
thesis: Make an unchanged image sequence support two coherent interpretations. Locate the strongest switch in meaning and identify the sonic event that causes it.
state: ◻(PictureMaster) is one frozen, timecoded video asset with decoded frame hashes. ◻(SoundVersion) contains voice, music, ambience, and alignment on the shared clock. ◻(CueClaim) links an audible event to a visible moment and the interpretation it may induce.
invariant: Lock frame count, order, dimensions, and cadence. Render both editions from the same video essence where practical. If re-encoding, verify decoded frames under the same representation. Preserve a silent playback as the control.
concurrency: Sound teams own separate mixes over one picture master. A picture change creates a new master and reopens alignment for both. At 100×, compare cue maps before rendering. Keep the mixer’s gain and loudness choices reviewable.
swarm: A picture editor locks a sequence. Two sound teams create clearly different readings. A mixer matches comparable playback conditions. A validator checks video identity. A fresh viewer compares the screenings without advance labels.
proof: Edit 25–35 seconds of a quiet housing complex, railway platform, or meeting hall. Score it once as a welcoming community space and once as a place of uneasy surveillance. Keep a common loudness target and test a voice-only or music-only crossover at the key cut.
fixture: Mix A and mix B attach to the same picture revision and decode to equal video frames. A one-frame retime or graphic insertion fails. Crossfade duration may change within the audio track.
critic: Ask the viewer to locate which heard cue changed their reading of the same shot. Counterbalance screening order if there are multiple viewers. Hold picture and compare playback at the same level.
inquiry: If both cuts produce the same reading, swap only narration over a common bed. If the difference depends on volume alone, level-match and test music harmony or perspective separately.
branch: Build a third soundtrack around selective silence and room tone. Keep the reference edit and compare what can be inferred with less overt framing.
deliver: One picture master, two playable editions, silent control, aligned stems, video identity report, and independent listening notes.
shared: Render the station encounter once. Play the exact picture with two audio accounts of the bell and departure. Keep any implied motive distinct from the event record.

title: Controlled text-to-video variation
line: Change one direction in the prompt and measure what changes on screen.
image: A bus hovering over a Paris crowd in a Dada-inspired generated image
gallery: Geometrically composed orange buses and figures on a blue street
A black-and-white charcoal-like image of a bus and pedestrians
sources: Describes the Queneau adaptation, text-to-video variations, and BCA exhibition.
Preserve prompt and render parameters with the output.
thesis: Find a controllable relationship between a changed instruction and a screen effect while the incident stays recognizable. Make stochastic variation visible enough to judge whether the proposed instruction actually has leverage.
state: ◻(EventAnchor) gives an essential action, role, prop, and observable cue. ◻(PromptDelta) records baseline prompt, one changed field, and intended effect. ◻(RenderAttempt) records engine/model revision, seed if supported, settings, conditioning inputs, output, and observation.
invariant: Preserve protected event anchors for accepted comparisons. Record what the engine actually lets you pin. Keep intervention, model, conditioning, and stochastic run differences distinct. If output is still-only, evaluate it as still imagery and deliver it under that milestone.
concurrency: Agents propose deltas against a frozen baseline. Reuse the same eligible seeds or sample schedule across conditions. Engine/version changes start a new experiment. At 100×, cap attempts per condition, deduplicate intent, and review a stratified sample rather than only the prettiest results.
swarm: A continuity owner defines event anchors. Variant authors design distinct interventions. A render operator pins available controls. A verifier records coverage and drift. A fresh critic compares unlabeled samples and traces the change to visible frames.
proof: Make a baseline of a small bus encounter. Test two interventions, one concerning camera stance and one concerning visual treatment. Use matched seeds where possible, or at least two samples per condition if reproducibility is limited. Keep duration and protected action stable. Use an executable procedural animatic if the requested generator is unavailable.
fixture: A variant with delta={camera: overhead} changes only the camera field in the manifest. A missing encounter or changed destination fails event coverage. A non-repeatable provider seed is recorded as an observed capability limit.
critic: Review clips at equal duration and display size. Report the rate at which the intended effect appears in inspected samples and the exact anchors that disappear. Separate observed samples from a claim about the generator in general.
inquiry: If control is weak, first strengthen the event conditioning without changing the style word. If style and action are entangled, compare a segmented generation pipeline against a single prompt. Preserve the least expensive method that supports the claim.
branch: Replace artist-name tokens with explicit material, framing, and motion descriptions. Test whether those words transfer the chosen perceptual effect across engines.
deliver: Playable samples or a clearly marked animatic, prompt-delta log, engine and seed metadata, comparison sheet, rejected drift examples, and the strongest reproducible checkpoint.
shared: Render the station seed under two named deltas and keep action coverage explicit. Test a treatment change and a camera change in separate conditions.

title: A mystery arranged by sextine
byline: Jacques Roubaud · novel first published in 1985
line: Permute six recurring motifs and make the mystery readable through their returns.
image: A paperback cover of La Belle Hortense with a blurred figure against green and red
sources: Identifies La Belle Hortense as the first novel in a cycle organized by a sextine constraint.
Catalogues the novel and reproduces its paperback cover.
Gives the six-position permutation used in this new proof.
Keep clues, reachability, and character knowledge explicit.
thesis: Make a recurring motif gain detective value on its return. Build a mystery in which formal ordering shapes what can be inferred and the reader can explain the solution from available clues.
state: ◻(Motif) has stable ID, visual or verbal signature, and permitted clue functions. ◻(Module) records its ordered motif appearances and reader knowledge on entry and exit. ◻(Permutation) maps one order into the next. ◻(Clue) has evidential support and reveal window.
invariant: For this new exercise apply the six-position sextine permutation [6,1,5,2,4,3] to the previous order. Use all six motifs once per module. Protect clue dependencies and keep the solution deducible before reveal. The formula is this prompt’s operational choice, alongside the documented sextine lineage.
concurrency: Module writers can work in parallel from the same motif grid. A clue move affecting when a reader can infer the answer triggers all later modules. At 100×, reject sequence and reachability violations before commissioning alternate scenes.
swarm: A combinatorial editor produces the six orders. A mystery designer maps clues and alternative explanations. Authors build local scenes around those motifs. A verifier checks permutation and deductive reachability. A fresh reader attempts the solution before reading the explanation.
proof: Write six short scenes or pages around a misplaced key and six motifs: key, bell, coat, bench, receipt, and locked door. Apply the permutation in all six modules. Make one motif act first as background and later as evidence. Give a reader enough to solve the immediate mystery without reciting the formula.
fixture: Starting [A,B,C,D,E,F], the next order is [F,A,E,B,D,C]. Six applications return the starting order. A module with a duplicate motif fails. A final reveal that depends on its own first appearance fails the clue test.
critic: Have a fresh reader name their leading explanation and which motif changed it before revealing the ending. Evaluate motif recurrence and mystery fairness separately.
inquiry: If the pattern feels like a checklist, preserve order and alter the role a motif plays. If the reveal feels unfair, move the earliest missing support within its legal slot or change the claim the clue must support.
branch: Translate the permutation to scene, light, or sound cues and compare when a viewer starts to recognize the return.
deliver: Six scenes or an equivalent playable sequence, motif and permutation matrix, clue graph, independent solution attempt, and editable canonical structure.
shared: Use the station episode as the first clue-bearing module. Keep the facts of the encounter intact. Repeat its six motifs across later investigative passages according to the permutation.

title: Film how readers build meaning
byline: Jean-Christophe Ribot · based around a poem by Jacques Roubaud
line: Show a reading change when a word, voice, or image arrives.
image: Close-up of a child speaking in Le Maki Mococo
sources: Association française pour la lecture, pedagogical dossier
Identifies Roubaud’s poem, Ribot’s film, and the reading exercise.
The director’s presentation of the film.
Treat the actual voice and listening response as evidence.
thesis: Make an interpretation visibly change while the poem stays fixed. Let the spectator hear a reader test an idea, encounter a cue, and try a different reading.
state: ◻(TextSegment) has revision, line ID, and display/read order. ◻(Cue) has channel, availability time, and linked line. ◻(ReaderResponse) has attributed speaker or fictional role, consent status, quoted span, current hypothesis, and next observation.
invariant: Keep text and cue release order explicit. Retain actual responses in context. Use consenting participants with the appropriate rights, or clearly fictional voice and animation. Preserve uncertainty and plausible alternate readings.
concurrency: Text/cue preparation and filming or staged animation share segment IDs. Changing the reveal time invalidates the response comparison. Consent scope changes invalidate dependent exports. At 100×, group hypotheses by cited cue and inspect distinct shifts before cutting more responses.
swarm: A reading designer selects a short original or authorized poem. A cue designer controls when sound, spelling, or an image appears. A recording or staging unit captures responses. An editor traces their change without rewriting the evidence. An independent reviewer audits whether the interpretation follows the released cue.
proof: Make a one-minute study of a short original poem with an unfamiliar animal or object name. Give readers sound first, then text, then an image. Record or stage two plausible guesses and one reconsideration. Use adults with consent or clearly fictional performers when appropriate for the resources.
fixture: A response recorded before cue Q cannot claim that Q was available at the time. Moving the image earlier defines a new condition. A reader’s words may be shortened only if their meaning and attribution remain auditable.
critic: Ask which clue shifted the reading, whether an alternate remained possible, and whether the cut preserves the order in which clues became available.
inquiry: If readers jump to one answer, hold text and delay or reduce the strongest visual cue. If no shift is visible, keep the cue order and add a chance for the reader to state why the new cue matters.
branch: Compare listening-first and reading-first conditions using the same poem, and preserve separate response traces.
deliver: Playable reading study, cue and response timeline, short poem or cleared source, consent/fiction ledger, and a reader-response audit.
shared: Give readers a brief original poem built around the bench, envelope, and bell. Release the image of the key after their first reading. Keep interpretations distinct from what physically happened.
